Lesson 4 · Anticipate next week

Simple regression and functional form

The audit supports further investigation. Operations now wants a simple planning relationship between a store’s usual delivery time and its stockout rate.

Business question → General theory → Worked application → Synthesis

First learn the definitions, notation, and logic of the method. Then use the shared case to work through the calculation and its interpretation.

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The motivating question

Long delivery cycles are a plausible source of replenishment pressure. The analyst returns to the 150 baseline store profiles and asks how their average rates vary with usual delivery time. We will fit a straight line, trace several predictions and residuals, and decide what that relationship contributes to planning. This introduces regression through a question about familiar stores and a familiar outcome.

Define a regression and its fitted values

General theory

Simple regression represents the conditional mean with a line

Yᵢ = α + βXᵢ + uᵢ; fitted value Ŷᵢ = a + bXᵢ

Y is the outcome, X the predictor, α the population intercept, and β the population slope. The error u represents variation around the specified relationship. A linear conditional-mean interpretation uses E[u | X] = 0. The fitted coefficients a and b are estimates obtained from observed data.

An overall mean gives the same prediction to every observation. Group means give different predictions to categories; a fitted line summarizes a continuous relationship using an intercept and slope.

Ordinary least squares minimizes squared prediction misses

Choose a and b to minimize Σ[Yᵢ − (a + bXᵢ)]²

Each residual is the vertical difference between an observation and its fitted value. Squaring gives larger misses greater influence and makes the loss nonnegative. The fitted line is the one minimizing the sum over the estimation sample. This optimization defines OLS before any uncertainty or causal interpretation is added.

The slope measures outcome units per additional predictor unit

b = Cov(X,Y) / Var(X); a = Ȳ − bX̄

The slope is positive when X and Y move together and negative when they move in opposite directions. Its magnitude is expressed in units of Y per unit of X. The intercept supplies the fitted value at X=0. Read both coefficients against the units and range of the data.

Choose what the regression is meant to represent

General theory

Description, prediction, and intervention ask different questions

The same fitted equation can support different tasks
PurposeQuestion
DescriptionHow does average Y vary with X in these records?
PredictionHow well can X anticipate an unknown Y?
InterventionWhat would happen to Y if we changed X?

Regression describes a conditional relationship. Predictive use additionally requires evidence about new observations; causal use requires a design that identifies an intervention effect. Begin with the question, then decide what evidence the fitted relationship needs. This lesson develops the equation and its fit; later lessons add validation and intervention designs.

A model can be nonlinear in X while remaining linear in its coefficients

  • A straight line chooses one global slope
  • Logs and powers change the predictor or outcome scale
  • Group means and local fits allow more flexible shape
  • Linear in coefficients includes a + b₁X + b₂X²

Parametric regression chooses a finite equation and estimates its coefficients. A quadratic bends in X but remains linear in a, b₁, and b₂, so ordinary least squares can fit its transformed columns. Local smoothing instead repeats small fits near each target. All approaches make choices about smoothness or grouping; flexible does not mean assumption-free. A power curve aXᵇ differs from an exponential curve a exp(bX).

OLS with an intercept balances residuals around the observed mean

Σeᵢ = 0; mean(Ŷ) = Ȳ; a + bX̄ = Ȳ

These are algebraic properties of the fitted sample, not assumptions that population errors disappear. They follow from minimizing squared residuals with an intercept. In simple regression the line passes through the point (X̄,Ȳ). The residuals may still show curvature or unequal spread, even though their sum is zero. The appendix derives these identities from the first-order equations.

Evaluate fit and choose a functional form

General theory

Residuals connect individual prediction misses with model fit

eᵢ = Yᵢ − Ŷᵢ; RMSE = √[Σeᵢ² / n]

A positive residual means the outcome exceeds its fitted value. Residual patterns can reveal systematic features missing from the chosen line. RMSE summarizes the squared misses in the original outcome units. On the estimation sample it describes training fit; performance on new observations requires separate evaluation.

R-squared describes the share of sample variation explained by OLS

SST = SSR + SSE; R² = 1 − SSE / SST

With an intercept, OLS partitions total squared variation around the sample mean into explained and residual components. SST is total variation, SSR explained variation, and SSE residual variation. R-squared is a relative measure of fit; RMSE reports an absolute error scale. Use both with the residual pattern.

Log transformations change the meaning of a slope

  • Level–level: one X unit corresponds to b Y units
  • Log–level: one X unit corresponds to approximately 100b% in Y
  • Level–log: 1% more X corresponds to approximately b/100 Y units
  • Log–log: 1% more X corresponds to approximately b% more Y

Choose a functional form from the relationship the model should express. Logs describe proportional changes and require positive values. The percentage interpretations are local approximations for small changes; exact finite changes use the log or exponential transformation. Compare predictions on a common outcome scale when assessing alternative forms.

Polynomial terms let the marginal association change with X

Ŷ = a + b₁X + b₂X²; slope at X = b₁ + 2b₂X

Read polynomial terms together through the predicted curve. The coefficient of X alone is not a constant slope once X² is included. Higher-order terms provide additional curvature. Plot the resulting predictions over the observed range and ask whether that flexibility captures a useful pattern.

Splines and local smoothing describe shape with different forms of flexibility

Linear spline: Ŷ = a + bX + c × max(X − knot, 0)

A linear spline changes the slope at a specified knot while keeping the curve continuous. Local smoothing instead fits relationships using nearby observations, often with distance-based weights. Both approaches help examine shape. Their tuning choices control how much detail the curve follows, so compare their implications on the same scale.

See the pieces behind the fit statistics

General theory

The variation decomposition separates fitted movement from residual movement

For each observation, yᵢ−ȳ = (ŷᵢ−ȳ)+eᵢ. Squaring produces an additional cross-term. In OLS with an intercept, the sum of that cross-term is zero, giving SST=SSR+SSE. The coloured lengths in the schematic are deviations, not sums of squares. The arithmetic in the retail application uses all 150 rows.

Logs express proportional changes rather than a fixed unit difference

  • Use positive quantities and state the units
  • A log difference is ln(Y₂/Y₁)
  • Multiplicative relationships become additive on a log scale
  • Choose the relationship, then inspect the transformed fit

Logging can make a proportional relationship easier to express and can reduce a long right tail. A skewed predictor does not by itself require a log: examine the conditional pattern and the meaning of proportional changes. For a logged predictor, the intercept corresponds to X=1 in the stated units. Zero has no finite logarithm; changing zero to a small constant changes the analysis and needs a substantive measurement rule.

Put delivery time and the rate on the same row

Worked application

Worked application: Baseline profiles · weeks 1–8 · all 150 stores. Apply the general method to the shared retail records below.

Each row contains a store’s usual delivery time, measured in days, and its average stockout percentage over weeks 1–8. Longer lead time is a store characteristic; the outcome summarizes eight weeks of operations. We are studying the relationship across stores.

Start by grouping stores with the same delivery time and plotting their mean rates. This shows the shape before asking a fitted equation to summarize it. The observed delivery times range from two to five days.

Build the relationship from increasingly specific predictions

Worked application

An overall mean gives every store the same prediction

The mean is the least-squares prediction when the model has only an intercept. It uses no information about delivery time. Plot the individual stores before summarizing them: stores with the same delivery time still have different stockout rates.

Group means adapt the prediction while sharing it within each group

The two group means are 11.158% for 71 stores and 14.166% for 79 stores. Every store in a group receives its group mean as its fitted value. Four delivery groups allow more detail: 10.23%, 11.92%, 13.14%, and 15.22%. A binned scatter summarizes mean Y at a chosen representative X; for continuous bins use the actual mean X or explicitly label a midpoint.

Check: which variation is hidden by the green points? They retain between-group differences but hide the distribution of individual rates inside each group. Showing the raw dots alongside the summaries preserves that information.

Covariance and predictor variance reconstruct the fitted line

Calculate with full precision; round only for display
StepValue
Mean delivery time; mean rate3.5733 days; 12.7423%
Sample covariance; sample X variance1.9413; 1.1993
Slope = covariance / variance1.61872 percentage points per day
Intercept = mean Y − slope × mean X6.95803%

The covariance has units of days times percentage points; the predictor variance has units of days squared. Their ratio therefore has units of percentage points per day. Both sample quantities use the same n−1 divisor, which cancels in the ratio. The intercept is a mathematical anchor at zero delivery days, outside the observed two-to-five-day range; use predictions in the observed range for the case.

Fit a line and read its units

Worked application

The regression predicts a store’s baseline percentage as an intercept plus a slope multiplied by delivery days. Least squares chooses the two coefficients to minimize the sum of squared residuals. A residual is the actual rate minus the prediction for that store.

Predicted baseline rate (%) = 6.96 + 1.62 × delivery days

For a four-day delivery cycle: 6.95803 + 1.61872 × 4 ≈ 13.43292%

The slope is 1.62 percentage points per additional delivery day. It describes the fitted difference across these baseline stores. Its unit is a change in percentage points, rather than a percentage change in the stockout rate.

Follow this calculation further →

Locate observations, fitted values, and residuals

Worked application

The fitted line passes through the means and leaves vertical residuals

S001 has actual rate 9.19643% and fitted rate 13.43292%, so its residual is -4.23649 percentage points. A positive residual would place a point above the line. The one-day slope describes movement along the line across stores; a residual describes one store’s departure from that line. The fitted line balances the signed residuals, while minimizing their squared total.

Trace fit through the stores it summarizes

Worked application

Five fitted store profiles
StoreLead daysActual baseline (%)Prediction (%)Residual (points)
S00149.2013.43-4.24
S00239.0211.81-2.80
S003314.2011.812.38
S004514.6415.05-0.41
S005414.0213.430.58

The root-mean-square residual is 1.60 percentage points. It describes how far these baseline store averages typically sit from the fitted line, giving larger misses more influence. This is a fit summary for the data used to estimate the coefficients.

Several stores can have the same delivery time and different outcomes. Their demand, promotion schedules, location, and operating practices differ. The line compresses that variation into one planning relationship. Its simplicity makes the comparison easy to explain and also shows what the next analysis should add.

The director can use this relationship to anticipate which delivery patterns tend to come with more stockout pressure. Measuring the effect of changing a delivery process would require an intervention comparison. That question enters later through the alert policy.

Account for what the fitted line represents

Worked application

Partition the variation around the mean

OLS variation decomposition
QuantitySum of squares
Total: Σ(y − mean y)²854.61
Explained: Σ(fitted − mean y)²468.22
Residual: Σ(y − fitted)²386.39

Total = explained + residual; R² = 1 − residual / total

R² is 0.55. It describes how much of this sample’s variation is represented by the fitted relationship. It does not state the causal importance of delivery time or the accuracy of forecasts for later weeks.

Keep goodness of fit in business units

MSE = SSE / n = 2.58; RMSE = √MSE = 1.60 points

RMSE is easier to interpret than squared error because it returns to the outcome’s units. Here the divisor n describes average squared fitting error; a residual-variance estimate for inference uses the residual degrees of freedom instead. Read a model report in order: sample, outcome units, coefficients, uncertainty, then fit.

Use the residual pattern to decide what to investigate

Worked application

Residual patterns reveal what a single slope leaves behind

Look for systematic movement of residual centres with delivery time, a change in their spread, and records far from the rest. Here each delivery group has substantial within-group variation. The mean residuals are small relative to that spread, consistent with the modest difference between the line and the four group means. The next lesson adds recorded operating conditions to explain more of the differences.

An unusual record and an influential record are different findings

Investigate records before changing the analysis sample
QuestionAction
Large residual: unusual Y given X?Check the recorded outcome, period, and denominator
Extreme X: unusual predictor value?Check units and the support for this comparison
Influence: does the fitted conclusion change?Refit with one record omitted as a sensitivity check

For the delivery slope, removing one store at a time identifies S081 as producing the largest absolute change: the slope moves from 1.61872 to 1.58727 points per day. This small observed change supports stability of that particular slope to single-record omission; it does not establish that the model captures every relevant feature.

The sensitivity fit is a diagnostic, not an instruction to delete the store. Verify a suspected error against its source, correct only an established error, and document any eligibility change. Accurate extreme observations can be important business cases. A positive residual alone does not show poor management.

Interpret transformations and compare their implied shapes

Worked application

Four equations express four different meanings of a slope

Same 150 stores; X = delivery days, Y = stockout rate in percent
ModelFitted equationRate-scale RMSE
Level–levelŶ = 6.958 + 1.619X1.605
Log–levelfitted ln Y = 2.062 + 0.130X1.602
Level–logŶ = 6.333 + 5.247ln X1.635
Log–logfitted ln Y = 2.007 + 0.425ln X1.618

For models fitted to log Y, the equation predicts the average log outcome. The RMSE column returns predictions to the rate scale using exp(fitted log Y) times the mean exp(log residual). This common scale permits a meaningful fit comparison. It does not make raw log-scale R² or squared errors directly comparable to their level-scale counterparts. All rows use the same stores.

A small log coefficient still needs an explicit unit calculation

Percentage points and percentage changes answer different questions
Model and changeExact fitted changeInterpretation
Level–level: +1 day1.619 pointsA percentage-point difference in the rate
Log–level: +1 day13.90%Relative rate change; about 13.0% by approximation
Level–log: X increases 1%0.0522 pointsSlope × ln(1.01)
Log–log: X increases 1%0.424%Relative change; about 0.425% by approximation

A rise from 10% to 11% is one percentage point and a 10% relative increase. These examples interpret the fitted equations; delivery time is observed only at whole-day values, so the 1% changes are mathematical illustrations of the model. For a log outcome, the finite-change percentages describe the exponentiated fitted-log scale and also the smearing-adjusted mean prediction when the smearing factor is held constant.

Check: if the log-log slope were −0.25, would 1% more X mean 25% less Y? No: the local approximation is 0.25% less Y. The coefficient is an elasticity, a ratio of proportional changes.

Different equations can produce similar fitted rates over the observed range

The curves nearly overlap here, and their training RMSEs range from about 1.60 to 1.64 points. Their interpretations still differ. A log-level equation is exponential in X; a log-log equation is a power curve. Choose a form for the question and plausible relationship, then assess it. Similar training fit is not evidence that the equations agree beyond the observed range.

Changing the outcome scale changes the shape of the same fitted equation

The left panel fits a straight line to log rates. Returning to rates produces a gently convex curve: a fixed proportional increase is a larger absolute increase when the starting rate is larger. The right panel multiplies exp(fitted log rate) by the common smearing factor 1.00862. Distances from these two curves have different units, so squared residuals on the two panels are not directly comparable. The underlying store records have not changed.

Continuous demand reveals shape that four delivery values cannot identify

We now hold the business case and 150 stores fixed but change the predictor to baseline demand. Its continuous values let us examine curve shape. The training RMSEs are 2.233, 2.213, and 2.212 points for the line, quadratic, and cubic. Curvature is modest relative to the spread among stores. These are demand models, so their coefficients must not be read as delivery-time slopes.

A cubic on delivery time has four coefficients for only four distinct X values, and reproduces the four group means. It does not supply observations between those values. The demand comparison provides a more useful setting for the original lesson’s curve discussion while keeping the same running example.

A quadratic slope changes with the predictor value

Ŷ = 12.416 + 0.988z − 0.168z²; z = (demand − 100)/10

The slope per demand-index point is (0.98757 + 2 × -0.16793z)/10. At demand 90 (z=−1), it is 0.1323 stockout percentage points per index point; at demand 120 (z=2), it is 0.0316. Read the linear and squared terms jointly. The division by ten converts the slope in z units back to the original index.

The displayed quadratic eventually turns downward near the upper edge. That is a feature of its fitted equation, not proof that raising demand reduces stockouts. Inspect the actual data density and restrict interpretation to supported comparisons. The cubic adds a 3b₃z² term to the derivative; the appendix shows the general calculation.

A spline changes its slope at a named knot while remaining continuous

Fit Ŷ = 12.339 + 1.125z − 0.964max(z−1,0), where z=(demand−100)/10. Below 110, the slope per index point is 0.1125; above 110 it is 0.0161. Both pieces give 13.464% at the knot, so there is no jump. The knot is chosen for this teaching comparison, not claimed as a policy boundary.

The hinge column switches on only after the knot

Compute each fitted value from the same three columns
Demandzmax(z−1,0)Fitted rate (%)
1000012.339
1101013.464
1202113.624

Below the knot, the hinge term contributes zero. Above it, the term adds a change in slope rather than a new intercept jump. At the knot it is exactly zero. Check: is the upper-segment slope the hinge coefficient alone? No: add the original slope and the hinge coefficient, then convert from z units to demand-index units.

A wider local neighborhood produces a smoother description

At each target demand, choose the nearest fraction of stores, weight closer observations more heavily, fit a small line, and evaluate it at the target. Repeat along the horizontal axis. The 35% curve follows more local movement; the 65% curve pools a broader neighborhood. At the boundary, the neighborhood lies mostly on one side, which affects how much local information is available.

Compare the broad pattern rather than interpreting every wiggle as a business mechanism. The code uses an explicit local-linear rule so the curves can be reproduced. It is a LOWESS-style exploration, not a separate prediction validation exercise. Lesson 6 tests candidate procedures on new observations.

Turn a simple relationship into a better question

Worked application

Use the fitted values as a rough benchmark for baseline store profiles within the observed two-to-five-day delivery range. Compare an unusually high residual with the store’s promotions and replenishment process. A residual can direct a useful conversation about what the one-variable model omitted.

The next lesson adds operating context to this same comparison. We will ask whether delivery time has the same fitted relationship in urban and other stores, and show how to calculate predictions for specified profiles.

Update the decision memo

Baseline stockout rates rise by about 1.62 percentage points per delivery day in the simple fitted comparison. Use the line to describe operating pressure and identify stores for review; next add the conditions that distinguish those stores.

Make the call

What is the difference between a positive residual and a positive delivery-time slope?

Compare your reasoning

A positive residual means a particular store’s actual rate is above its prediction. A positive slope means the fitted rate rises as delivery time rises across the comparison.

The bigger picture

A regression is a specified way to summarize how an outcome varies with predictors. The same reasoning applies to cost, demand, and performance relationships. Define the variables, choose the functional form, interpret its slope correctly, and inspect the residuals before deciding what the fitted relationship can contribute.

After your decision: open the known answer

The shared generator includes delivery time, location, demand, promotions, and store differences. The single-variable line summarizes their observed combination in the baseline profiles.
